subject: ss-ctvs
title: Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery
curriculum: NMC Competency-Based MCh Cardiothoracic and Vascular Surgery (CTVS) Curriculum / NBEMS NEET-SS Surgical Group (CTVS)
examPattern: NEET-SS Surgical Group paper (150 MCQs, 40 percent feeder MS General Surgery and 60 percent super-speciality). Within the super-speciality share, cardiothoracic and vascular surgery is heavily tested across cardiopulmonary bypass and myocardial protection, coronary revascularisation (CABG indications, conduits, on-pump vs off-pump), acquired valvular surgery (stenosis, regurgitation, repair vs replacement, prostheses, endocarditis), thoracic aorta (aneurysms, Stanford A/B dissections, TEVAR), congenital heart disease (shunts, cyanotic spells, TOF, TGA, single ventricle pathways, coarctation), thoracic surgery (lung cancer staging and resections, mediastinal compartments and tumours, pleura, empyema, bronchiectasis), and mechanical circulatory support (ECMO, IABP, LVAD, heart/lung transplantation). Weight follows MCh CTVS university papers, the INI-SS important-topic list and exam-pyq overlays.
book: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 22nd Edition 2025 (Elsevier) Chapters 57 (Heart Transplantation), 58 (Lung Transplantation), 102 (Aortic Disease), 110 (Lung, Chest Wall, Pleura, and Mediastinum), 111 (Acquired Heart Disease: Coronary Artery Disease), 112 (Acquired Heart Disease: Valvular), 113 (Congenital Heart Disease), 114 (Pulmonary Embolism), 115 (Percutaneous Heart Procedures), 116 (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation); STS/AATS/ACC/AHA and EACTS/ESC Guidelines

sections.name: Cardiopulmonary Bypass, Mechanical Circulatory Support, and Transplantation

modules.name: Cardiopulmonary Bypass Circuits, Cannulation and Anticoagulation

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Technique of myocardial revascularization: Conventional on-pump cardiopulmonary bypass)

mustKnow.fact: Cardiopulmonary bypass diverts deoxygenated venous return from the right atrium or venae cavae through a membrane oxygenator and returns oxygenated blood under arterial pressure into the ascending aorta.

Systemic anticoagulation requires unfractionated heparin at an initial loading dose of 300 to 400 units per kilogram to achieve an activated clotting time exceeding 480 seconds before initiating cardiopulmonary bypass.

Following decannulation from bypass, protamine sulfate reverses heparin at a ratio of 1 to 1.3 mg of protamine per 100 units of initial heparin, titrated to return activated clotting time to baseline.
Patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia or antithrombin III deficiency who require urgent bypass receive bivalirudin or fresh frozen plasma with antithrombin concentrate respectively.
Arterial cannulation is conventionally placed in the distal ascending aorta proximal to the innominate artery takeoff, while peripheral cannulation employs the common femoral or axillary artery.

Venous drainage utilizes a two-stage single cannula in the right atrium and inferior vena cava for coronary procedures, or bicaval cannulation with snaring for open right heart or transseptal procedures.

Left ventricular venting via the right superior pulmonary vein or aortic root decompresses the left heart, preventing ventricular distention, subendocardial ischemia, and pulmonary venous hypertension.

Systemic perfusion during hypothermic bypass targets a cardiac index of 2.2 to 2.4 L/min/m2 and mean arterial pressure between 50 and 80 mmHg to preserve renal, cerebral, and mesenteric end-organ blood flow.

modules.name: Myocardial Protection, Cardioplegia Solutions and Hypothermia

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Technique of myocardial revascularization: Conventional on-pump cardiopulmonary bypass)

mustKnow.fact: Aortic cross-clamping isolates the coronary circulation, producing immediate global myocardial ischemia that requires chemical arrest and hypothermia to suppress myocardial metabolic demand and ATP consumption.

Hyperkalemic cardioplegia induces rapid diastolic electromechanical arrest by depolarizing the myocyte resting membrane potential from negative 90 millivolts to negative 50 millivolts, inactivating fast voltage-gated sodium channels.

Antegrade cardioplegia delivered into the aortic root or direct coronary ostia relies on an intact, competent aortic valve, whereas aortic insufficiency causes cardioplegia to regurgitate and distend the left ventricle.

Retrograde cardioplegia is delivered directly into the coronary sinus through an inflatable balloon catheter, providing effective homogeneous distribution even in the presence of severe multivessel proximal coronary occlusions.
Coronary sinus pressure during retrograde infusion must strictly not exceed 40 to 50 mmHg to avoid traumatic rupture or thrombosis of the coronary sinus and myocardial edema.

Cold blood cardioplegia administered in a 4 to 1 blood-to-crystalloid ratio provides intermittent oxygen delivery, buffers acidosis, and is readministered every 15 to 20 minutes during prolonged ischemic cross-clamp periods.

Del Nido cardioplegia uses a single-dose crystalloid-to-blood ratio of 4 to 1 containing lidocaine and magnesium, providing safe, sustained myocardial protection for up to 60 to 90 minutes of cross-clamp time.

Terminal warm reperfusion or hot shot cardioplegia administered just prior to aortic cross-clamp release replenishes depleted myocardial substrate, washes out toxic acid metabolites, and accelerates functional recovery.

modules.name: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump: Mechanics, Timing and Indications

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Mechanical complications of acute myocardial infarction; Postoperative management)

mustKnow.fact: The intra-aortic balloon catheter is inserted percutaneously via the common femoral artery and positioned in the descending thoracic aorta with its tip 1 to 2 centimetres distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.
Balloon inflation occurs precisely at the dicrotic notch on the arterial pressure waveform, corresponding to aortic valve closure, augmenting diastolic coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure.

Balloon deflation occurs immediately prior to ventricular systole during the isovolumetric contraction phase, markedly reducing left ventricular afterload, myocardial wall stress, and myocardial oxygen demand.

Severe aortic regurgitation is an absolute contraindication to intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation because diastolic balloon inflation worsens regurgitant volume into the left ventricle and produces acute ventricular dilatation.

Thoracic aortic dissection and severe aortoiliac occlusive disease represent absolute or strong relative contraindications to intra-aortic balloon insertion due to the risk of aortic wall perforation and catastrophic limb ischemia.

The primary clinical indications for intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation include cardiogenic shock refractory to inotropes, acute post-infarction ventricular septal defect, acute papillary muscle rupture, and failure to wean from bypass.

Limb ischemia caused by femoral artery thrombosis or vessel occlusion is the most frequent major complication of intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation, requiring surveillance of pedal pulses and compartmental pressures.

Weaning from counterpulsation is initiated once inotropic requirements stabilize and cardiac index exceeds 2.2 L/min/m2, progressively reducing pump assistance ratios from 1 to 1 down to 1 to 2 and 1 to 3 prior to removal.

modules.name: Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation: VA vs VV Circuits and Management

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 116 (Advances in extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: Techniques, applications, and management)

mustKnow.fact: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation drains deoxygenated blood from the venous system and returns oxygenated blood into the arterial system, providing both biventricular hemodynamic support and pulmonary gas exchange.

Venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation drains and reinfuses blood entirely within the venous circulation, providing isolated respiratory gas exchange without direct mechanical cardiac hemodynamic augmentation.

Peripheral venoarterial cannulation via the femoral artery and vein generates retrograde arterial flow toward the aortic valve, increasing left ventricular afterload and risking acute left ventricular distention, pulmonary edema, and intracardiac stasis.

Harlequin syndrome, or North-South syndrome, occurs during femoral venoarterial ECMO when poorly oxygenated native cardiac stroke volume perfuses the brain and right arm while retrograde ECMO perfuses the lower extremities.

To prevent acute lower extremity ischemia during femoral arterial cannulation, a dedicated 6 to 8 French distal perfusion cannula is placed in the superficial femoral artery to maintain antegrade distal limb flow.

Left ventricular venting strategies in patients receiving venoarterial ECMO include percutaneous atrial septostomy, placement of an intra-aortic balloon pump, an Impella axial flow catheter, or surgical apex drainage.

Anticoagulation on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation circuits requires continuous unfractionated heparin targeting an anti-factor Xa level of 0.3 to 0.7 units/mL or an activated partial thromboplastin time of 50 to 70 seconds.
Weaning from venovenous ECMO is confirmed by turning the sweep gas flow entirely off while mechanical ventilatory parameters remain within lung-protective limits with normal arterial blood gases.

modules.name: Ventricular Assist Devices: LVAD Mechanics, Inflow, Outflow and Complications

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111; STS/INTERMACS Guidelines

mustKnow.fact: Left ventricular assist devices are continuous-flow rotary or centrifugal blood pumps implanted as a bridge to transplantation, bridge to candidacy, bridge to myocardial recovery, or permanent destination therapy.
The LVAD inflow cannula is cored and sewn into the true left ventricular apex directed along the long axis toward the mitral valve, avoiding suction against the ventricular septum or lateral wall.

The LVAD outflow graft is anastomosed in an end-to-side bevelled fashion to the ascending aorta, positioned to ensure laminar flow into the systemic arterial tree without kinking or aortic wall impingement.

Right ventricular failure occurs in 20 to 30 percent of patients following LVAD implantation due to increased venous return, leftward shift of the interventricular septum, and unmasked pre-existing right ventricular dysfunction.

Continuous high shear stress across rotary impeller blades cleaves high-molecular-weight von Willebrand factor multimers, causing acquired von Willebrand disease and recurrent gastrointestinal arteriovenous malformation bleeding.
Pump thrombosis manifests as elevated pump power spikes, serum lactate dehydrogenase exceeding 2.5 to 3 times the upper limit of normal, hemoglobinuria, and acute heart failure.
Driveline exit-site infection is the most frequent infectious complication of durable assist devices, requiring aggressive wound dressing protocols and culture-directed antibiotic suppression.

Long-term outpatient management requires antiplatelet therapy combined with warfarin targeting an international normalized ratio of 2.0 to 3.0 to balance the competing risks of thromboembolism and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.

modules.name: Heart Transplantation: Recipient Selection, Biatrial vs Bicaval Technique and Rejection

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 57 (Heart transplantation)

mustKnow.fact: Indications for orthotopic heart transplantation include end-stage New York Heart Association class IV heart failure refractory to optimal guideline-directed medical and device therapy with a peak VO2 below 12 to 14 mL/kg/min.

Fixed pulmonary hypertension with pulmonary vascular resistance exceeding 4 to 5 Wood units refractory to vasodilator challenge is an absolute contraindication to isolated orthotopic heart transplantation due to acute donor right ventricular failure.

Donor heart preservation utilizes hypothermic static cold storage with crystalloid cardioplegic solutions, with safe cold ischemic time strictly restricted to under 4 to 6 hours to prevent primary graft dysfunction.

The modern bicaval orthotopic transplantation technique anastomoses the donor left atrium, inferior vena cava, superior vena cava, pulmonary artery, and ascending aorta, preserving anatomical right atrial geometry.

Compared with the historical Lower-Shumway biatrial technique, bicaval anastomosis significantly reduces the incidence of postoperative tricuspid regurgitation, sinus node dysfunction, and permanent pacemaker requirement.

Because the transplanted donor heart is surgically denervated, resting heart rate is elevated between 90 and 110 beats per minute, the heart is unresponsive to atropine, and carotid sinus massage produces no bradycardia.

Acute cellular rejection is surveillance-screened using surveillance endomyocardial biopsies of the right ventricular septum, graded histologically from grade 0R to 3R according to International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation criteria.

Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is an accelerated, diffuse, concentric intimal proliferation affecting epicardial and intramyocardial coronary vessels, representing the leading cause of late graft failure and death beyond 1 year post-transplant.

modules.name: Lung Transplantation: Single, Bilateral, Anastomotic Technique and PGD

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 58 (Lung transplantation)

mustKnow.fact: Indications for lung transplantation include end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, cystic fibrosis, and idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension with projected 2-year survival below 50 percent.

Cystic fibrosis and non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis require mandatory bilateral sequential lung transplantation to prevent lethal cross-contamination of the newly implanted donor allograft from the remaining native septic lung.
The surgical sequence of lung implantation begins with the bronchial anastomosis, followed by the pulmonary arterial anastomosis, and finishes with the left atrial cuff anastomosis.

The donor and recipient bronchus must be transected as short as possible, strictly within one cartilage ring of the lobar takeoff, and wrapped with vascularized donor peribronchial tissue or omentum to avoid ischemic dehiscence.

Primary graft dysfunction is a severe form of acute ischemic-reperfusion lung injury developing within 72 hours of transplantation, characterized by noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, diffuse alveolar damage, and hypoxemia.

Primary graft dysfunction is graded from grade 0 to grade 3 based on the ratio of PaO2 to FiO2 and the presence of diffuse infiltrates on chest radiography, with grade 3 defined by a PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 200.

Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome represents the clinical manifestation of chronic lung allograft dysfunction, characterized by irreversible, progressive obstructive airflow decline with FEV1 dropping below 80 percent of post-transplant baseline.

Maintenance immunosuppressive therapy following lung transplantation consists of a triple-drug regimen combining a calcineurin inhibitor such as tacrolimus, an antimetabolite like mycophenolate mofetil, and corticosteroids.

modules.name: Cardiac Trauma: Penetrating, Blunt, Pericardial Tamponade and Emergency Resuscitative Thoracotomy

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 36 (Management of acute trauma; Thoracic trauma)

mustKnow.fact: Beck triad of acute cardiac tamponade consists of hypotension, jugular venous distention with elevated central venous pressure, and muffled heart sounds, accompanied by pulsus paradoxus exceeding 10 mmHg.

The right ventricle is the most frequently injured cardiac chamber in penetrating thoracic trauma due to its broad anterior anatomical position immediately beneath the sternum and anterior chest wall.

Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma demonstrates anechoic fluid separation between the visceral epicardium and parietal pericardium, providing immediate bedside identification of hemopericardium.

Emergency department resuscitative thoracotomy is indicated in patients with penetrating thoracic trauma who suffer witnessed cardiac arrest or lose vital signs with less than 15 minutes of prehospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

Anterolateral thoracotomy in the left fourth or fifth intercostal space followed by transverse sternal transection into a clamshell thoracotomy provides rapid, bilateral exposure of the heart and great vessels.
Immediate opening of the pericardium is performed longitudinal and anterior to the phrenic nerve to evacuate clotted hemopericardium, relieve tamponade, and permit internal cardiac massage.

Penetrating ventricular lacerations are temporarily controlled with digital pressure, balloon Foley catheter occlusion, or skin staples, followed by definitive repair with pledgeted horizontal mattress polypropylene sutures.

Blunt cardiac injury ranges from asymptomatic myocardial contusion to free wall rupture, with troponin I and continuous 12-lead electrocardiographic monitoring mandatory for at least 24 hours to detect lethal arrhythmias.

sections.name: Coronary Artery Disease and Surgical Revascularisation

modules.name: CABG Indications: Multivessel CAD, Left Main, Diabetes and SYNTAX Score

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Indications for coronary artery revascularization)

mustKnow.fact: Coronary artery bypass grafting provides a definitive long-term survival advantage over percutaneous coronary intervention in patients with significant left main coronary stenosis exceeding 50 percent.

Surgical revascularization is preferred for three-vessel coronary artery disease with high anatomic complexity defined by a SYNTAX score greater than 22, achieving significantly lower major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular event rates.

In diabetic patients with multivessel coronary disease, the FREEDOM trial demonstrated that CABG confers superior 5-year all-cause mortality reduction and lower myocardial infarction rates compared with drug-eluting stents.

In patients with ischemic cardiomyopathy and left ventricular ejection fraction of 35 percent or lower, the STICH trial proved that surgical revascularization plus medical therapy improves 10-year all-cause survival over medical therapy alone.

Complete revascularization, defined as grafting every diseased major coronary territory with diameter 1.5 mm or greater and stenosis 50 percent or greater, substantially reduces long-term repeat revascularization and ischemic events.

The Heart Team approach involving a cardiac surgeon, interventional cardiologist, and clinical cardiologist is a Class I guideline recommendation for guiding revascularization decisions in complex multivessel coronary disease.

In acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction, emergency CABG is indicated for ongoing refractory ischemia, failed PCI with persistent symptoms, or mechanical complications such as ventricular septal rupture.
Dual antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statin therapy are initiated postoperatively to prevent vein graft thrombosis and stabilize atherosclerotic plaques, improving graft patency and survival.

modules.name: Conduit Selection: LIMA, RIMA, Radial Artery and Saphenous Vein

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Technique of myocardial revascularization)

mustKnow.fact: The left internal mammary artery anastomosed to the left anterior descending artery is the gold standard conduit in CABG, yielding superior 10-year patency rates exceeding 90 to 95 percent and significant survival prolongation.

Bilateral internal mammary artery grafting improves long-term survival in younger patients, but skeletonized harvesting is mandatory in diabetics and obese individuals to prevent sternal devascularization and deep sternal wound infection.

The radial artery provides an excellent arterial conduit with 10-year patency exceeding 85 percent when grafted to a target coronary vessel with high-grade proximal native stenosis of 70 to 80 percent or greater.
Grafting a radial artery to a coronary vessel with native stenosis under 70 percent predisposes the arterial graft to competitive native flow and string sign atrophic narrowing.

Preoperative Allen test or ultrasound modified Allen test is mandatory before radial artery harvest to verify complete palmar arch patency from the ulnar collateral circulation, avoiding acute hand digital ischemia.
Calcium channel blocker therapy such as diltiazem is routinely administered for at least 6 months postoperatively to suppress radial artery smooth muscle spasm and maintain graft patency.

The great saphenous vein remains the most widely utilized conduit for multivessel revascularization, with 10-year patency of approximately 50 to 60 percent due to intimal hyperplasia and accelerated graft atherosclerosis.

Endoscopic saphenous vein harvesting significantly reduces leg wound infections, wound dehiscence, hematoma formation, and postoperative leg pain compared to traditional open longitudinal harvest techniques.

modules.name: On-Pump vs Off-Pump CABG: Techniques, Haemodynamics and Trials

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting)

mustKnow.fact: Off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting achieves revascularization on the beating heart without cardiopulmonary bypass or aortic cross-clamping using mechanical myocardial tissue stabilizers and intracoronary shunts.

Mechanical stabilizers utilize suction pods to immobilize the target coronary segment, while intracoronary shunts maintain continuous distal myocardial perfusion and create a bloodless operative field during delicate microvascular suturing.

Heart verticalization and deep pericardial retraction stitches to expose the posterior and lateral coronary vessels cause transient hemodynamic instability through right ventricular compression and decreased venous return.

Trendelenburg positioning, right pleural cavity opening, and judicious temporary vasopressor administration maintain mean arterial pressure and cardiac output during posterior obtuse marginal revascularization.

Anaortic or no-touch off-pump CABG utilizes in situ composite arterial grafting without any ascending aortic side-biting clamping or manipulation, dramatically decreasing perioperative stroke in patients with severe aortic atheroma.

The randomized ROOBY and CORONARY trials demonstrated comparable 30-day mortality between on-pump and off-pump surgery, but off-pump CABG carried a lower number of completed grafts and slightly higher 1-year repeat revascularization.
Off-pump CABG is particularly advantageous in patients with porcelain aorta, severe chronic kidney disease, advanced cirrhosis, and high bleeding diathesis.

Emergency conversion from off-pump to on-pump bypass occurs in 2 to 5 percent of cases due to intractable ventricular arrhythmias, refractory hemodynamic collapse, or profound regional ischemia, requiring immediate emergent cannulation.

modules.name: Post-Infarction Ventricular Septal Defect and Free Wall Rupture

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Mechanical complications of acute myocardial infarction)

mustKnow.fact: Ventricular septal rupture complicates 0.2 to 0.5 percent of acute myocardial infarctions, typically developing 3 to 7 days post-infarction as coagulative necrosis and neutrophilic infiltration weaken the infarcted myocardium.

Anterior myocardial infarctions from LAD occlusion produce apical muscular septal defects that are usually simple and direct, whereas inferior infarctions produce complex, serpiginous basal posterior septal defects.
Clinical presentation features sudden hemodynamic collapse, biventricular failure, and a harsh, loud holosystolic murmur with a palpable thrill best appreciated along the left lower sternal border.
Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography establish the diagnosis, demonstrating left-to-right color Doppler flow across the muscular septum and right ventricular systolic volume overload.

Preoperative hemodynamic stabilization utilizes an intra-aortic balloon pump to reduce left ventricular afterload, lower left-to-right shunting, and augment coronary perfusion pressure while preparing for emergency surgery.

Surgical repair employs an infarct exclusion patch technique via a left ventriculotomy through the infarcted myocardium, securing a Dacron or bovine pericardial patch with pledgeted sutures anchored to healthy non-infarcted septal tissue.
Concomitant coronary artery bypass grafting to non-infarcted ischemic territories is performed to improve operative survival and preserve residual ventricular functional capacity.

Left ventricular free wall rupture occurs in 1 to 2 percent of transmural infarctions, presenting as acute pseudoaneurysm, electromechanical dissociation, or catastrophic cardiac tamponade requiring emergent surgical patch repair.

modules.name: Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation and Acute Papillary Muscle Rupture

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Mechanical complications of acute myocardial infarction)

mustKnow.fact: Acute papillary muscle rupture is a catastrophic post-infarction mechanical complication occurring 2 to 7 days after transmural infarction, precipitating pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.

The posteromedial papillary muscle ruptures 6 to 10 times more frequently than the anterolateral papillary muscle because it has a single solitary arterial blood supply from the posterior descending coronary artery.

In contrast, the anterolateral papillary muscle is protected against isolated ischemic necrosis and rupture by a dual coronary blood supply derived from both the left anterior descending and left circumflex arteries.

Physical examination may reveal a soft, early systolic murmur rather than a classic holosystolic murmur because acute severe regurgitation into an unprepared, non-compliant left atrium leads to early left atrial and ventricular pressure equalization.

Emergency echocardiography confirms flail mitral leaflet motion, eccentric regurgitant jetting, and hyperdynamic left ventricular contractility, with prominent pulmonary capillary wedge V-waves on right heart catheterization.
Emergency mitral valve replacement with chordal preservation is the definitive surgical procedure of choice for complete papillary muscle transection due to necrotic, non-suturable papillary tissue.

Chronic functional ischemic mitral regurgitation is caused by adverse left ventricular remodeling, posterior leaflet tethering, and apical displacement of the papillary muscles, rather than intrinsic valvular leaflet pathology.

Surgical treatment of severe chronic secondary ischemic mitral regurgitation involves restrictive undersized mitral annuloplasty with a rigid complete ring combined with surgical coronary revascularization.

modules.name: Left Ventricular Aneurysm and Surgical Remodeling: Dor Procedure

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Mechanical complications of acute myocardial infarction; Left ventricular aneurysm)

mustKnow.fact: True left ventricular aneurysm consists of a thinned, scarred fibrous ventricular wall containing all three layers of the heart (endocardium, fibrotic myocardium, and epicardium), having a broad neck that expands dyskinetically during systole.

Pseudoaneurysm represents a contained myocardial rupture bounded only by the overlying adherent parietal pericardium and thrombus, characterized by a narrow neck, high rupture risk, and an urgent indication for surgical resection.

True left ventricular aneurysms occur most commonly in the anteroapical myocardium following transmural myocardial infarction caused by acute occlusion of the left anterior descending coronary artery.

The classic clinical triad of left ventricular aneurysm comprises congestive heart failure from loss of effective stroke volume, recurrent angina from increased wall tension, and refractory ventricular arrhythmias originating from border-zone scar tissue.

Mural thrombus develops within the stagnant akinetic or dyskinetic apex in up to 50 percent of cases, presenting a significant risk for systemic and cerebral thromboembolism that requires preoperative systemic anticoagulation.

The Dor procedure, or endoventricular circular patch plasty, reconstructs left ventricular geometry by incising the aneurysm, evacuating intraventricular mural thrombus, and placing an endoventricular purse-string suture at the transition zone.

An oval Dacron or pericardial patch is secured across the neo-apex to exclude akinetic scar tissue and restore an elliptical physiological ventricular cavity, with surgical ventricular restoration targeting an end-systolic volume index of 50 to 60 mL/m2.
Concomitant cryoablation or surgical endocardectomy of the arrhythmogenic scar border zone is performed in patients with documented ventricular tachycardia to abolish re-entrant electrical circuits.

modules.name: Reoperative CABG: Sternal Re-entry, Patent LIMA and Strategy

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Technical aspects of reoperative coronary artery bypass grafting)

mustKnow.fact: Preoperative evaluation for redo cardiac surgery requires mandatory high-resolution chest computed tomography to evaluate the retrosternal space, proximity of the ascending aorta, and location of patent internal mammary artery grafts.

Injury to a patent left internal mammary artery graft during sternal re-entry results in catastrophic anteroseptal myocardial infarction, intractable ventricular fibrillation, and a reported mortality exceeding 30 to 50 percent.

If a patent internal mammary artery is positioned immediately beneath the posterior sternal table or midline crossing, peripheral femoral-femoral bypass is established before sternotomy to permit decompression and rapid hypothermic cooling.

Sternal re-entry utilizes an oscillating saw for the anterior cortex followed by careful elevation and division of the posterior cortex, with dissection maintained strictly against the retrosternal periosteum.

Dissection in redo CABG is selectively restricted to anatomical sites necessary for cannulation, cross-clamping, and constructing target coronary anastomoses, avoiding unnecessary pericardial adhesiolysis.

In the presence of a patent functional LIMA graft, the LIMA must be carefully identified and clamped during cardioplegia infusion to prevent warm systemic blood from washing out cardioplegia and warming the anterior wall.

Atherosclerotic old vein grafts contain friable, unorganized debris and must not be touched or manipulated until cross-clamping to prevent lethal atheroembolism into the distal coronary microcirculation.
Prior failed vein grafts are ligated after new conduits are established to eliminate competing flow and eliminate the source of recurrent late embolization.

modules.name: Minimally Invasive and Hybrid Coronary Revascularisation: MIDCAB and TECAB

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 111 (Minimally invasive direct coronary artery bypass; Robotic totally endoscopic CABG; Hybrid coronary surgery)

mustKnow.fact: Minimally invasive direct coronary artery bypass grafting performs an in situ LIMA-to-LAD anastomosis on the beating heart through a 4 to 6 centimetre left anterior mini-thoracotomy in the fourth intercostal space.

Totally endoscopic coronary artery bypass revascularization utilizes robotic surgical telemanipulator arms introduced through 8 mm thoracic trocars without any thoracotomy incision, requiring remote femoral port-access bypass.

Hybrid coronary revascularization combines surgical internal mammary artery grafting to the left anterior descending artery with percutaneous drug-eluting stenting of non-LAD culprit coronary vessels (circumflex or right coronary artery).

The clinical rationale for hybrid revascularization is combining the established 20-year survival and patency durability of LIMA-to-LAD with the low invasiveness of percutaneous coronary intervention for non-LAD lesions.
Hybrid procedures may be performed as a concurrent single-stage procedure in a dedicated hybrid operating room suite with angiographic capabilities or staged sequentially over several days.
When staging hybrid procedures, performing surgical LIMA-LAD first allows immediate antiplatelet loading with P2Y12 inhibitors during subsequent PCI without increasing surgical bleeding risks.

Intraoperative transit-time flow measurement is mandatory during minimally invasive CABG, with a pulsatility index below 5.0 and mean graft flow greater than 15 to 20 mL/min confirming technical anastomotic adequacy.

Exclusion criteria for minimally invasive and robotic LIMA harvest include morbid obesity, previous left thoracotomy with pleural obliteration, small calcified intramyocardial LAD target, and severe peripheral vascular disease.

sections.name: Acquired Valvular Heart Disease and Endocarditis

modules.name: Aortic Stenosis: Hemodynamics, Indications, SAVR and TAVR

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Acquired heart disease: Valvular; Aortic valve disease) and Ch 115 (Percutaneous heart procedures)

mustKnow.fact: Severe high-gradient aortic stenosis is hemodynamically defined by an aortic valve area of 1.0 cm2 or less (or indexed valve area below 0.6 cm2/m2), mean transvalvular gradient of 40 mmHg or greater, or peak jet velocity of 4.0 m/s or greater.

The classic symptomatic triad of severe aortic stenosis comprises angina, syncope on exertion, and dyspnea from heart failure, with average survival without surgical relief dropping to 5 years, 3 years, and 2 years respectively.

Asymptomatic patients with severe aortic stenosis have a Class I indication for aortic valve intervention if left ventricular ejection fraction falls below 50 percent, or Class IIa if undergoing other cardiac surgery or very severe peak velocity exceeds 5.0 m/s.

Surgical aortic valve replacement is performed via median sternotomy or minimally invasive right anterior minithoracotomy, entering the aortic root through a transverse or hockey-stick aortotomy placed 1 cm above the sinotubular junction.

Patient-prosthesis mismatch occurs when the effective orifice area of the implanted prosthetic valve is abnormally small relative to patient body surface area, defined as an indexed effective orifice area of 0.85 cm2/m2 or less.

Aortic root enlargement techniques such as the Nicks, Manouguian, or Konno procedures enlarge a small aortic annulus by 1 to 2 valve sizes, preventing patient-prosthesis mismatch and elevated postoperative gradients.

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement is preferred over SAVR in patients aged 80 years or older or those with high or prohibitive surgical risk (STS-PROM score greater than 8 percent), transfemorally delivering balloon-expandable or self-expanding valves.

SAVR is strongly recommended over TAVR in patients younger than 65 years or with life expectancy greater than 20 years, bicuspid aortic valve anatomy, severe multi-level left ventricular outflow tract calcification, or associated aortopathy.

modules.name: Aortic Regurgitation: Pathophysiology, Indications, Valve Sparing Root Repair

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Aortic Regurgitation or Insufficiency) and Ch 102 (Aortic disease)

mustKnow.fact: Chronic aortic regurgitation causes severe combined left ventricular volume and pressure overload, inducing eccentric hypertrophy and progressive ventricular dilatation to accommodate massive total stroke volumes.

Severe aortic regurgitation is echocardiographically quantified by a regurgitant volume of 60 mL or greater, regurgitant fraction of 50 percent or greater, effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.30 cm2 or greater, and vena contracta width exceeding 6 mm.

Surgical intervention is indicated in asymptomatic severe chronic aortic regurgitation when resting left ventricular ejection fraction is 55 percent or lower, or end-systolic dimension exceeds 50 mm (or indexed LVESD greater than 25 mm/m2).

Acute severe aortic regurgitation resulting from aortic dissection or infective endocarditis produces sudden ventricular volume overload into a non-compliant ventricle, causing premature mitral valve closure and rapid cardiovascular collapse.

The Bentall procedure replaces the aortic valve, aortic root, and ascending aorta with a composite mechanical or tissue valved conduit, with direct reimplantation of coronary ostia as buttons (modified button Bentall technique).

Valve-sparing aortic root replacement by the David reimplantation technique preserves the native tricuspid or bicuspid aortic valve leaflets inside a cylindrical or Valsalva Dacron graft, stabilizing the dilated annulus and sinotubular junction.

The Yacoub remodeling technique replaces the sinuses of Valsalva with a scalloped Dacron graft without annular stabilization, carrying a slightly higher late recurrent regurgitation rate in patients with extensive annuloaortic ectasia.

Aortic valve repair requires careful assessment of geometric leaflet height (normal 9 to 10 mm) and effective coaptation height greater than 9 mm, using central leaflet plication or free-margin resuspension.

modules.name: Mitral Stenosis: Rheumatic Pathology, Wilkins Score and Surgical Commissurotomy

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Mitral Stenosis)

mustKnow.fact: Rheumatic heart disease is the predominant etiology of mitral stenosis worldwide, characterized by progressive fibrous leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, chordal shortening, and subvalvular fusion producing a fish-mouth orifice.

Severe mitral stenosis is hemodynamically defined by a mitral valve area of 1.5 cm2 or less (very severe if 1.0 cm2 or less), mean transmitral diastolic pressure gradient of 5 to 10 mmHg or greater, or pulmonary artery systolic pressure exceeding 50 mmHg.

The Wilkins echocardiographic score grades mitral valve morphology from 1 to 4 across four components: leaflet mobility, leaflet thickening, subvalvular thickening, and valvular calcification, generating a total score between 4 and 16.

Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy is the first-line intervention in symptomatic severe mitral stenosis with favourable anatomy defined by a Wilkins score of 8 or less in the absence of left atrial thrombus or moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation.

Left atrial appendage transesophageal echocardiography is mandatory before balloon commissurotomy or surgical repair to definitively exclude intracardiac thrombus, which represents an absolute contraindication to percutaneous dilation.

Open surgical mitral commissurotomy is indicated in patients with pliable leaflets, mild subvalvular disease, and Wilkins score under 10 who fail or have contraindications to balloon commissurotomy (such as dense left atrial appendage thrombus).

In patients with severe valvular calcification, extensive subvalvular chordal fusion, and concomitant moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation (Wilkins score greater than 11), surgical mitral valve replacement is the procedure of choice.

Preservation of posterior chordopapillary connections during mitral valve replacement preserves left ventricular geometry, avoids posterior wall blowout, and significantly improves postoperative left ventricular systolic performance.

modules.name: Mitral Regurgitation: Carpentier Classification, Annuloplasty and Leaflet Resection

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Mitral Regurgitation)

mustKnow.fact: Carpentier functional classification categorizes mitral regurgitation based on leaflet motion: Type I has normal leaflet motion (annular dilation or leaflet perforation), Type II has excessive leaflet motion (prolapse or flail), and Type III has restricted leaflet motion.

Carpentier Type III is subdivided into Type IIIa, where leaflet motion is restricted during both diastole and systole (rheumatic disease), and Type IIIb, where leaflet motion is restricted predominantly during systole (ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy).

Primary degenerative mitral regurgitation is caused by fibroelastic deficiency or Barlow disease with myxomatous degeneration, presenting with chordal elongation or rupture and leaflet prolapse affecting the P2 middle scallop most commonly.

Surgical mitral valve repair is the gold standard for severe primary degenerative regurgitation, achieving operative mortality below 1 percent and superior long-term survival and ejection fraction preservation compared to valve replacement.
Quadrangular or triangular resection of the prolapsing posterior middle scallop followed by leaflet re-approximation and reconstruction restores smooth leaflet coaptation geometry.

Artificial neochordae construction utilizing expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (Gore-Tex) sutures anchored from the papillary muscle head to the free margin of prolapsing leaflets provides effective non-resectional repair.

Full prosthetic ring annuloplasty is mandatory in every degenerative mitral valve repair to remodel annular geometry, reduce annular circumference, and prevent late recurrent regurgitation from annular dilatation.

Systolic anterior motion of the anterior mitral leaflet with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction is a potential repair complication caused by excessive leaflet height, anterior displacement of the coaptation line, or an undersized annuloplasty ring.

modules.name: Tricuspid Valve Disease: Functional Regurgitation, Annuloplasty Rings and Ebstein

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Tricuspid Regurgitation and Other Right-Sided Valvular Disease)

mustKnow.fact: Secondary or functional tricuspid regurgitation accounts for over 85 to 90 percent of cases, caused by left-sided heart disease, pulmonary hypertension, and right ventricular dilatation leading to severe tricuspid annular dilatation.

Concomitant tricuspid annuloplasty is a Class I recommendation during left-sided valve surgery in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation, or Class IIa for mild-to-moderate regurgitation with tricuspid annular diameter exceeding 40 mm (or 21 mm/m2).
Tricuspid annular dilatation occurs primarily along the anterior and posterior leaflet attachments, whereas the septal leaflet annulus remains relatively constant due to fibrous skeleton attachments.

Rigid or semi-rigid prosthetic ring annuloplasty yields superior long-term freedom from recurrent tricuspid regurgitation compared with suture bicuspidization or purse-string annuloplasty techniques (such as the De Vega or Kay repairs).

Sutures along the anteroseptal commissure and triangle of Koch must be placed with extreme caution to avoid injuring the atrioventricular node and bundle of His, which lie immediately superior to the coronary sinus ostium.

When tricuspid valve replacement is required, a bioprosthetic valve is strongly preferred over a mechanical valve because the low-pressure, low-velocity right-sided circulation predisposes mechanical tricuspid valves to catastrophic thrombosis.

Carcinoid heart disease causes dense fibrous endocardial plaques on the tricuspid valve leaflets and subvalvular apparatus, resulting in rigid, retracted, non-coapting leaflets requiring surgical replacement with bioprostheses.

In adult Ebstein anomaly with severe regurgitation, modern surgical reconstruction utilizes the cone repair technique to delaminate adhered leaflet tissue from the right ventricular wall and construct a 360-degree circumferential leaflet cone.

modules.name: Prosthetic Valve Selection: Mechanical vs Bioprosthetic, Thrombosis and Anticoagulation

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Prosthetic Valves)

mustKnow.fact: Modern mechanical bileaflet pyrolytic carbon valves offer lifelong mechanical durability without structural deterioration, but require lifelong systemic anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists such as warfarin.

Bioprosthetic bovine pericardial or porcine tissue valves offer low intrinsic thrombogenicity and do not require lifelong anticoagulation, but undergo age-dependent structural valve deterioration from calcification and leaflet tearing within 10 to 15 years.

Mechanical valves are recommended in patients younger than 50 years undergoing aortic replacement or younger than 65 years undergoing mitral replacement who have no contraindications to long-term anticoagulation.

Bioprosthetic valves are recommended in patients aged 65 years or older undergoing aortic replacement or aged 70 years or older undergoing mitral replacement, and in patients with lifestyle or occupational contraindications to anticoagulation.

Target international normalized ratio for a mechanical bileaflet aortic valve in the absence of risk factors is 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0), whereas a mechanical mitral valve or aortic valve with thromboembolic risk factors requires a target INR of 3.0 (range 2.5 to 3.5).

Direct oral anticoagulants like dabigatran or rivaroxaban are absolutely contraindicated in patients with mechanical heart valves because the RE-ALIGN trial proved they cause significantly higher thromboembolism and bleeding rates compared to warfarin.

Acute mechanical valve thrombosis presents with muffled prosthetic clicks, acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, and high transvalvular gradients, requiring emergent cinefluoroscopy and surgical thrombectomy or systemic thrombolysis.

Prosthetic paravalvular leak occurs in 2 to 5 percent of surgical valve replacements due to localized suture disruption or infective endocarditis, causing hemolytic anemia from erythrocyte shear stress or refractory heart failure.

modules.name: Infective Endocarditis: Duke Criteria, Urgent Surgical Indications and Abscess Reconstruction

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 112 (Endocarditis)

mustKnow.fact: The modified Duke criteria establish the diagnosis of infective endocarditis using major criteria (persistent positive blood cultures with typical organisms, echocardiographic evidence of vegetation or abscess) and minor criteria.

Transesophageal echocardiography has a sensitivity exceeding 90 to 95 percent for detecting endocardial vegetations and is superior to transthoracic echocardiography for diagnosing perivalvular abscesses and prosthetic valve dehiscence.

The three primary Class I indications for urgent cardiac surgery in native valve endocarditis are refractory heart failure from acute severe regurgitation, uncontrolled infection (perivalvular abscess, fistula, enlarging vegetation), and prevention of recurrent embolic events.

Vegetation size exceeding 10 mm on mobile mitral or aortic leaflets associated with a prior embolic episode, or isolated persistent vegetation larger than 15 mm despite appropriate antibiotics, represents an urgent surgical indication.

Aortic root abscess manifests electrocardiographically as progressive PR interval prolongation or new-onset complete heart block due to inflammatory extension into the atrioventricular node within the membranous septum.
Surgical radical debridement of all infected and necrotic annular tissue until completely healthy bleeding tissue is exposed is the paramount principle for eradicating perivalvular root abscesses.

Extensive aortic root destruction and aorto-cavitary fistulae require complete root replacement utilizing a cryopreserved aortic homograft, bovine pericardial conduit, or freestyle stentless bioprosthesis.

Following surgical intervention for active infective endocarditis, a full 4 to 6 week course of tailored intravenous antimicrobial therapy is continued starting from the date of surgical tissue debridement.

modules.name: Surgical Management of Atrial Fibrillation: Cox-Maze IV and LAA Exclusion

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 115 (Atrial fibrillation ablation)

mustKnow.fact: The surgical Maze procedure eliminates atrial fibrillation by creating transmural lines of electrical conduction block that interrupt macro-reentrant electrical wavelets while preserving sinus node depolarization and atrioventricular transport.

The modern Cox-Maze IV procedure replaces historical cut-and-sew surgical incisions with bipolar radiofrequency energy and cryoablation clamps to create identical full-thickness transmural lesion sets rapidly and safely.

The Cox-Maze IV lesion set includes bilateral pulmonary vein antral isolation, a connecting roof line, an inferior floor line creating a posterior left atrial box lesion, a mitral isthmus line to the mitral annulus, and right atrial ablation lines.

Cryoablation applies temperatures down to negative 60 degrees Celsius for 2 minutes to ablate the mitral isthmus and coronary sinus without risking coronary artery thermal injury or circumflex artery occlusion.

Concomitant surgical atrial fibrillation ablation during mitral valve surgery is a Class I guideline recommendation, significantly increasing 1-year sinus rhythm restoration rates to over 70 to 80 percent without increasing operative mortality.

The left atrial appendage is the source of intracardiac thrombus in over 90 percent of patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation and over 50 percent of patients with rheumatic mitral valve disease.

Complete left atrial appendage exclusion is achieved surgically using epicardial clip application (such as the AtriClip), surgical stapler excision, or internal suture closure, avoiding residual stumps larger than 1 cm.

The LAAOS III trial proved that surgical occlusion of the left atrial appendage during routine cardiac surgery in patients with atrial fibrillation reduces the 3-year risk of ischemic stroke and systemic embolism by 33 percent.
mustKnow.source: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 115; LAAOS III Trial

sections.name: Thoracic Aorta, Dissection, Aneurysms and Pulmonary Embolism

modules.name: Acute Type A Aortic Dissection: Stanford Classification and Emergency Ascending Repair

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 102 (Aortic disease; Dissection/intramural hematoma)

mustKnow.fact: Stanford Type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta regardless of the primary intimal tear entry site, whereas Stanford Type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.

In DeBakey classification, Type I involves the ascending aorta and extends into the aortic arch and descending aorta; Type II is confined strictly to the ascending aorta; and Type III involves only the descending aorta.

Untreated acute Stanford Type A dissection carries an upfront mortality of approximately 1 to 2 percent per hour during the first 24 to 48 hours, reaching nearly 50 percent mortality by 48 hours from pericardial rupture or coronary malperfusion.

Preoperative medical management targets immediate blood pressure reduction with intravenous beta-blockers such as esmolol or labetalol to achieve a systolic blood pressure between 100 and 120 mmHg and heart rate below 60 bpm.

Emergency surgical repair consists of open distal anastomosis under hypothermic circulatory arrest with antegrade selective cerebral perfusion, resecting the primary intimal tear and replacing the ascending aorta with a Dacron tube graft.

The aortic valve is preserved and resuspended at the commissures using pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures in up to 70 to 80 percent of patients when the aortic root and valve leaflets are structurally normal.

Extensive root dissection, annuloaortic ectasia, or primary intimal tear extending into the sinuses of Valsalva mandates composite aortic root replacement with coronary button reimplantation (Bentall procedure).

Distal false lumen obliteration is achieved using biological glues (such as gelatin-resorcin-formalin or BioGlue) and Teflon felt strip reinforcement of the inner and outer aortic walls prior to graft anastomosis.

modules.name: Type B Aortic Dissection: Medical Therapy, Complicated Presentation and TEVAR

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 102 (Dissection/intramural hematoma)

mustKnow.fact: Uncomplicated acute Type B aortic dissection is managed primarily with medical impulse control therapy utilizing intravenous beta-blockers and vasodilators to maintain systolic blood pressure between 100 and 120 mmHg.

Complicated acute Type B aortic dissection is defined by hemodynamic instability, rapid aortic expansion, refractory pain or hypertension, rupture or contained rupture, or end-organ malperfusion (visceral, renal, or lower extremity ischemia).

Thoracic endovascular aortic repair is the primary treatment of choice for complicated acute Type B aortic dissection, sealing the primary entry tear with a stent-graft to depressurize the false lumen and expand the compressed true lumen.

A proximal seal landing zone of at least 20 mm of non-dissected healthy aortic wall is required, frequently requiring coverage of the left subclavian artery with pre-emptive carotid-subclavian bypass to prevent posterior stroke and left arm ischemia.

In uncomplicated Type B dissection, the INSTEAD and INSTEAD-XL trials demonstrated that TEVAR in the subacute phase (15 to 90 days) promotes positive aortic remodeling and significantly reduces 5-year aorta-specific mortality.

Retrograde Type A aortic dissection occurs in 1 to 4 percent of patients undergoing TEVAR for Type B dissection, representing a lethal device-related complication caused by stent-graft spring wire trauma to the fragile aortic arch.

Spinal cord ischemia and paraplegia occur in 2 to 6 percent of thoracic endovascular procedures, mitigated by cerebrospinal fluid drainage, maintaining mean arterial pressure above 80 to 90 mmHg, and staging extensive coverage.

Aortic intramural hematoma and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcers represent variants of acute aortic syndromes with high risk of progression to overt dissection or transmural rupture requiring urgent surveillance and endovascular intervention.

modules.name: Ascending and Aortic Arch Aneurysms: Sizing, Hemiarch and Total Arch Replacement

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 102 (Aortic aneurysm)

mustKnow.fact: Surgical resection is indicated for asymptomatic ascending thoracic aortic aneurysms when maximal external diameter reaches 5.5 cm in non-syndromic patients, or 5.0 cm in patients with bicuspid aortic valve and risk factors.

In genetic connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome, surgical intervention is recommended at an aortic diameter of 5.0 cm (or 4.5 cm with family history of early dissection or rapid growth exceeding 0.5 cm per year), and 4.5 cm in Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

Ascending aortic aneurysms extending to the proximal aortic arch are repaired with hemiarch replacement under moderate hypothermic circulatory arrest at 24 to 28 degrees Celsius, beveling the distal graft along the underside of the transverse arch.
Total arch replacement involves resecting the entire aortic arch and reimplanting the brachiocephalic vessels as an island button or via separate branched prosthetic graft limbs.

Bilateral antegrade selective cerebral perfusion via direct cannulation of the right axillary/innominate and left common carotid arteries delivers cold oxygenated blood at 10 to 12 mL/kg/min, significantly reducing neurological morbidity during arch reconstruction.

The conventional elephant trunk procedure leaves a free-floating redundant Dacron tube graft suspended in the proximal descending aorta, facilitating safe second-stage thoracotomy or open surgical completion.

The frozen elephant trunk hybrid technique combines total arch replacement with an integrated distal stented endograft deployed antegradely into the descending thoracic aorta under direct vision during a single-stage operation.

Cerebral oximetry using near-infrared spectroscopy provides continuous non-invasive cerebral tissue oxygen saturation monitoring during circulatory arrest, with a drop greater than 20 percent from baseline triggering immediate perfusion adjustment.

modules.name: Thoracoabdominal Aortic Aneurysms: Crawford Classification and Paraplegia Protection

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 102 (Aortic aneurysm)

mustKnow.fact: The Crawford classification categorizes thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms from extent I to extent V based on proximal origin, distal termination, and visceral vessel involvement.
Crawford Extent I involves most of the descending thoracic aorta from above the sixth intercostal space down to the upper abdominal aorta above the renal arteries.

Crawford Extent II is the most extensive and carries the highest risk of ischemic paraplegia, extending from the proximal descending thoracic aorta down past the renal arteries to the aortic bifurcation.

Crawford Extent III involves the lower descending thoracic aorta below the sixth intercostal space into the abdominal aorta; Extent IV is confined to the abdominal aorta below the diaphragm; and Extent V involves the lower thoracic aorta and upper abdominal aorta sparing the infrarenal aorta.

Ischemic spinal cord injury and paraplegia result from cross-clamping of critical intercostal and lumbar radiculomedullary feeding arteries, particularly the artery of Adamkiewicz (arteria radicularis magna) arising between T8 and L1.

Spinal cord protection multimodal strategy includes continuous cerebrospinal fluid drainage maintaining CSF pressure below 10 mmHg, distal aortic perfusion via left heart bypass, permissive hypothermia, and reattachment of critical intercostal arteries from T8 to T12.
Selective cold crystalloid or blood visceral and renal perfusion during cross-clamping preserves mesenteric and renal cellular architecture, minimizing acute kidney injury and bowel ischemia.

Motor evoked potentials and somatosensory evoked potentials provide real-time intraoperative spinal cord neurophysiological monitoring, where a 50 percent amplitude reduction immediately alerts the surgeon to acute spinal ischemia.

modules.name: Acute Massive Pulmonary Embolism: Surgical Pulmonary Embolectomy Indications and Technique

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 114 (Pulmonary embolism: Acute and chronic; Acute pulmonary embolism)

mustKnow.fact: Massive or high-risk pulmonary embolism is clinically defined by sustained systemic arterial hypotension (systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg or a drop of 40 mmHg or greater for more than 15 minutes) or cardiogenic shock.

Submassive or intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism features normotension but demonstrates objective evidence of right ventricular strain on echocardiography or CT, accompanied by elevated myocardial necrosis biomarkers (cardiac troponin or BNP).

Surgical pulmonary embolectomy is indicated in massive acute PE with absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolytic therapy, failed systemic thrombolysis with persistent refractory shock, or documented mobile thrombus in transit through right heart chambers.

Surgical embolectomy is performed under full cardiopulmonary bypass via median sternotomy on a beating heart with normothermia, entering the main pulmonary artery through a longitudinal arteriotomy 1 cm above the pulmonary valve.

Thrombi are systematically extracted from the main trunk, right pulmonary artery, and left pulmonary artery branches using fine forceps, suction catheters, and gentle manual pleural compression of the lungs.

Aortic cross-clamping and cardioplegic arrest are avoided if possible, but are utilized if concomitant closure of a patent foramen ovale or surgical repair of an intracardiac right atrial thrombus is required.

Modern surgical series for massive pulmonary embolism report operative survival exceeding 85 to 90 percent when embolectomy is performed promptly prior to irreversible cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest.

Placement of an inferior vena cava filter is indicated postoperatively only in patients with recurrent embolism despite therapeutic anticoagulation or persistent absolute contraindications to systemic anticoagulation.

modules.name: CTEPH: Pathophysiology, Workup and Pulmonary Thromboendarterectomy

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 114 (Chronic pulmonary embolism and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension)

mustKnow.fact: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension develops in 1 to 4 percent of pulmonary embolism survivors, characterized by organized, fibrotic intravascular thrombi obstructing elastic pulmonary arteries and secondary microvascular arteriopathy.

The diagnostic definition of CTEPH requires mean pulmonary arterial pressure exceeding 20 mmHg at rest with pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 15 mmHg or lower and pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 2 Wood units following 3 months of anticoagulation.

Ventilation-perfusion lung scintigraphy is the screening modality of choice for CTEPH, with a normal V/Q scan completely ruling out chronic thromboembolic disease with a negative predictive value approaching 100 percent.

Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy is the gold standard, potentially curative surgical treatment for CTEPH, performed via median sternotomy under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest at 18 to 20 degrees Celsius.

Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest periods are strictly limited to 20-minute intervals separated by 10 minutes of reperfusion, providing a completely bloodless operative field essential for visualizing delicate endarterectomy planes.

The surgeon dissects the true endarterectomy cleavage plane within the media layer of the pulmonary artery, systematically tracking into subsegmental branches bilaterally rather than performing simple embolectomy.

Reperfusion pulmonary edema is a unique postoperative complication developing within 72 hours in revascularized lung segments, manifesting as localized alveolar infiltrates and severe hypoxemia requiring protective ventilation and ECMO support.

Successful thromboendarterectomy achieves immediate, dramatic reductions in pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressures, reversing right ventricular remodeling and providing 10-year survival exceeding 75 to 80 percent.

modules.name: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: Neurogenic, Venous, Arterial and First Rib Resection

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 110 (Thoracic outlet syndrome)

mustKnow.fact: Thoracic outlet syndrome encompasses compression of the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus trunks, subclavian artery, and subclavian vein) within the interscalene triangle, costoclavicular space, or retropectoral space.

Neurogenic TOS accounts for greater than 90 to 95 percent of cases, caused by compression of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1 nerve roots) leading to paresthesias in an ulnar nerve distribution and thenar muscle atrophy.

Venous TOS (Paget-Schroetter syndrome or effort thrombosis) accounts for 3 to 5 percent of cases, presenting with acute arm swelling, cyanosis, and heaviness following vigorous upper extremity repetitive exertion.

Arterial TOS accounts for approximately 1 percent of cases, almost always associated with a congenital cervical rib or anomalous first rib causing subclavian artery stenosis, post-stenotic aneurysm, and distal microembolization.

Provocative diagnostic physical examination maneuvers include the elevated arm stress test (Roos test), Adson test (palpation of radial pulse while rotating head and taking a deep inspiration), and Wright hyperabduction test.

For acute Paget-Schroetter venous thrombosis, catheter-directed catheter-directed pharmacomechanical thrombolysis is initiated emergently, followed by prompt first rib resection during the same hospitalization to decompress the thoracic outlet.

Surgical thoracic outlet decompression requires complete resection of the first rib combined with anterior and middle scalenectomy, performed via a transaxillary, supraclavicular, or infraclavicular approach.

Iatrogenic surgical complications during first rib resection include injury to the long thoracic nerve (winged scapula), phrenic nerve (diaphragm paralysis), brachial plexus lower trunk, or subclavian vessels.

modules.name: Blunt Thoracic Aortic Injury: Isthmus Rupture, Grading and Endovascular Repair

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 102 (Aortic trauma) and Ch 36 (Management of acute trauma)

mustKnow.fact: Blunt thoracic aortic injury occurs most commonly at the aortic isthmus, immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery at the attachment of the ligamentum arteriosum, where mobile aortic arch joins fixed descending aorta.
High-speed frontal or lateral motor vehicle collisions with rapid deceleration produce sudden displacement and torsional shear forces across the tethered aortic isthmus.

Chest radiography screening signs of aortic injury include mediastinal widening exceeding 8 cm on an upright film, loss of the aortic knob contour, left apical pleural cap, tracheal deviation to the right, and left hemothorax.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography of the chest is the gold standard imaging modality of choice, establishing the diagnosis with a sensitivity and negative predictive value approaching 100 percent.

The Society for Vascular Surgery injury grading scale categorizes injuries into: Grade I (intimal tear), Grade II (intramural hematoma), Grade III (pseudoaneurysm), and Grade IV (free aortic rupture).

Grade I intimal tears are managed conservatively with medical impulse control therapy (beta-blockers maintaining mean arterial pressure below 80 mmHg) and serial follow-up CT surveillance without surgical repair.

Thoracic endovascular aortic repair is the definitive first-line standard of care for Grade II to IV injuries, achieving significantly lower operative mortality and paraplegia rates compared to open thoracotomy repair.

In polytrauma patients with severe concomitant intracranial hemorrhage or pelvic hemorrhage, aortic repair can be safely delayed for 24 to 48 hours under strict beta-blocker pressure control while prioritizing life-threatening non-aortic injuries.

sections.name: Congenital Heart Disease and Paediatric Cardiac Surgery

modules.name: Acyanotic Shunts: ASD Types, VSD Anatomy and Surgical Patch Closure

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Congenital heart disease; Lesion overview: Defects Associated With Increased Pulmonary Blood Flow)

mustKnow.fact: Atrial septal defects are anatomically classified into ostium secundum (70 percent, fossa ovalis defect), ostium primum (15 to 20 percent, partial AV canal), sinus venosus (superior or inferior caval junction), and rare coronary sinus defects.

Superior vena cava type sinus venosus ASD is strongly associated with anomalous partial drainage of the right superior pulmonary vein into the superior vena cava or right atrium, requiring surgical baffling (Warden procedure).

Ventricular septal defects are categorized into perimembranous (80 percent, beneath septal leaflet of tricuspid valve), muscular, doubly committed subarterial (supracristal), and inlet (atrioventricular canal type) defects.

The bundle of His runs along the posteroinferior margin of perimembranous VSDs on the left ventricular side, requiring surgical patch sutures to be placed safely away on the right ventricular aspect of the crest or on the tricuspid valve leaflet.

Doubly committed subarterial (supracristal) VSDs require surgical closure regardless of shunt volume because prolapse of the right coronary aortic valve leaflet leads to progressive aortic regurgitation and sinus of Valsalva aneurysm.

Surgical patch closure of perimembranous and inlet VSDs is performed under cardiopulmonary bypass via a transatrial approach through the tricuspid valve, avoiding a ventriculotomy to preserve ventricular contractility.

Surgical ligation and division of patent ductus arteriosus is indicated for large hemodynamically significant shunts in premature infants failing medical indomethacin or acetaminophen therapy, or when ductal anatomy is unsuitable for transcatheter occlusion.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve curves directly around the patent ductus arteriosus from anterior to posterior, making it vulnerable to traction or clip injury causing postoperative vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.

modules.name: Coarctation of the Aorta and Interrupted Aortic Arch: Repair Techniques

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Aortic Arch Anomalies)

mustKnow.fact: Coarctation of the aorta is a discrete luminal narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta typically located at the insertion of the ductus arteriosus immediately distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.
Bicuspid aortic valve is present in 50 to 85 percent of patients with coarctation of the aorta, and Berry aneurysms of the circle of Willis occur in up to 10 percent.

Clinical hallmarks of coarctation include upper extremity hypertension, diminished or delayed femoral pulses (radiofemoral delay), and rib notching on chest radiography along ribs 3 to 8 due to dilated intercostal collateral vessels.

Neonatal critical coarctation depends on ductal patency, presenting with sudden metabolic acidosis, cardiogenic shock, and differential cyanosis upon spontaneous ductus closure, requiring immediate continuous prostaglandin E1 infusion.
Surgical resection with extended end-to-end anastomosis via a left posterolateral thoracotomy in the fourth intercostal space is the surgical treatment of choice in neonates and young infants.

Paradoxical postoperative hypertension and mesenteric arteritis (postcoarctectomy syndrome) result from acute baroreceptor resetting and sympathetic hyperactivation, managed aggressively with intravenous sodium nitroprusside or beta-blockers.

Interrupted aortic arch is complete anatomical luminal discontinuity between the ascending and descending aorta, categorized into Celoria-Patton Type A (distal to left subclavian), Type B (between left carotid and left subclavian), and Type C (between innominate and left carotid).

Type B interrupted aortic arch is strongly associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) in over 50 percent of cases, presenting with severe hypocalcemia, thymic aplasia, and an associated large posterior malalignment VSD.

modules.name: Tetralogy of Fallot: Anatomy, Cyanotic Spells, BT Shunt and Primary Complete Repair

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Cyanotic Congenital Heart Disease; Conotruncal Anomalies)

mustKnow.fact: The four anatomical components of Tetralogy of Fallot result from anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular (outlet) septum: large non-restrictive subaortic VSD, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Hypercyanotic spells (tet spells) result from acute infundibular muscular spasm or peripheral systemic vasodilation increasing right-to-left shunting, treated by knee-chest positioning, oxygen, intravenous morphine, beta-blockers, and phenylephrine.

The modified Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt connects the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral pulmonary artery via an interposition Gore-Tex tube graft to provide palliative pulmonary blood flow in severely cyanotic neonates unsuitable for primary repair.
Primary complete surgical repair is routinely performed electively at 3 to 6 months of age under cardiopulmonary bypass with bicaval cannulation and cardioplegic arrest.

Surgical repair consists of extensive infundibular muscle resection, closure of the subaortic VSD using a Dacron or bovine pericardial patch via a transatrial approach, and relief of pulmonary outflow tract stenosis.

A transannular patch crossing the pulmonary valve annulus is required when the pulmonary annulus z-score is less than negative 2 to negative 3, relieving obstruction at the expense of creating obligate free pulmonary regurgitation.

Preoperative coronary angiography is critical to identify an anomalous left anterior descending artery arising from the right coronary artery crossing the anterior RVOT (occurring in 5 percent of cases), which strictly precludes a transannular incision.

Late postoperative morbidity is dominated by chronic pulmonary regurgitation causing progressive right ventricular dilatation, requiring transcatheter or surgical pulmonary valve replacement when indexed RV end-diastolic volume exceeds 160 mL/m2.

modules.name: Transposition of the Great Arteries: Arterial Switch Operation (Jatene Procedure)

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Conotruncal Anomalies; Transposition of the Great Arteries)

mustKnow.fact: Complete dextro-transposition of the great arteries (d-TGA) is characterized by ventriculoarterial discordance, where the aorta arises anteriorly from the morphologic right ventricle and the pulmonary artery arises posteriorly from the morphologic left ventricle.

The pulmonary and systemic circulations run in parallel rather than in series, making survival dependent on bidirectional mixing sites across a patent ductus arteriosus, atrial septal defect, or ventricular septal defect.

Immediate neonatal stabilization utilizes continuous intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion to maintain ductal patency, followed by bedside balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) if cyanosis is profound and mixing is inadequate.

The arterial switch operation (Jatene procedure) is the anatomical surgical repair of choice, performed within the first 2 to 3 weeks of life before the left ventricle regresses and loses the ability to support systemic afterload.

The key technical step of the Jatene operation is harvesting the coronary artery ostia as wide aortic buttons and mobilizing and transferring them without tension, torsion, or kinking into the neo-aorta (neoaortic root).
The LeCompte maneuver translocates the bifurcated pulmonary artery confluence anterior to the ascending aorta before constructing the neo-pulmonary artery anastomosis.

If an infant with d-TGA with intact ventricular septum presents beyond 3 to 4 weeks of life with regressed left ventricle, a two-stage switch is performed: initial pulmonary artery banding and systemic-to-pulmonary shunt to retrain the LV, followed by the arterial switch.

Congenitally corrected transposition (l-TGA) features both atrioventricular and ventriculoarterial discordance, managed anatomically with the double switch operation combining an atrial switch (Senning or Mustard) with an arterial switch.

modules.name: Single Ventricle Pathway: HLHS, Norwood, Bidirectional Glenn and Fontan Operations

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Single Ventricle; Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome)

mustKnow.fact: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is characterized by hypoplasia or atresia of the aortic valve and mitral valve, hypoplastic ascending aorta, and severe hypoplasia of the left ventricle incapable of supporting systemic circulation.

Stage 1 palliation (Norwood procedure) is performed during the first week of life, creating a neo-aorta utilizing the pulmonary root and a homograft patch, an unrestricted atrial septectomy, and a source of controlled pulmonary blood flow.

Pulmonary blood flow during Stage 1 is established via a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt (innominate artery to pulmonary artery) or a Sano shunt (right ventricle to pulmonary artery conduit using non-valved Gore-Tex).

Stage 2 palliation (bidirectional Glenn operation or superior cavopulmonary anastomosis) is performed at 3 to 6 months of age, dividing the superior vena cava and anastomosing it directly end-to-side to the right pulmonary artery.

The bidirectional Glenn unloads the single ventricle by removing superior vena caval volume work while providing passive, non-pulsatile cerebral venous blood flow directly into the pulmonary vascular bed.

Stage 3 completion (Fontan operation) is performed at 2 to 4 years of age, directing inferior vena caval deoxygenated return directly into the pulmonary artery via an extracardiac Gore-Tex conduit or lateral tunnel.

A small 4 to 5 mm fenestration is placed in the Fontan conduit to provide a right-to-left decompression pop-off, maintaining cardiac output and reducing systemic venous pressure at the expense of mild systemic cyanosis.

Late complications of the failing Fontan circulation include protein-losing enteropathy, plastic bronchitis, hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis (Fontan-associated liver disease), and refractory atrial tachyarrhythmias.

modules.name: Truncus Arteriosus and Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Connection (TAPVC)

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Persistent Arterial Trunk; Abnormalities of Venous Drainage)

mustKnow.fact: Truncus arteriosus features a single common great arterial trunk overriding the ventricular septum that supplies the systemic, pulmonary, and coronary circulations, classified by Collett-Edwards into Types I through IV.

Complete neonatal repair of truncus arteriosus requires separation of the pulmonary arteries from the trunk, patch closure of the large malalignment VSD, and reconstruction of right ventricular to pulmonary artery continuity using a valved homograft or conduit (Rastelli technique).

Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection is characterized by all four pulmonary veins draining into the systemic venous circulation rather than the left atrium, categorized by Darling into supracardiac (Type I, 50 percent), cardiac (Type II, 25 percent), infracardiac (Type III, 20 percent), and mixed (Type IV).

In supracardiac TAPVC, the confluence of pulmonary veins drains via a vertical vein into the innominate vein and superior vena cava, producing the classic snowman or figure-of-eight sign on chest radiography.

Infracardiac TAPVC drains via a descending vertical vein through the esophageal hiatus into the portal vein or inferior vena cava, almost invariably presenting with severe anatomical venous obstruction and profound neonatal pulmonary edema.

Obstructed TAPVC is an absolute surgical emergency requiring immediate emergent repair on cardiopulmonary bypass, as mechanical balloon septostomy or medical management cannot relieve the intrapulmonary venous hypertension.

Surgical repair consists of creating a wide, tension-free side-to-side anastomosis between the pulmonary venous confluence and the posterior left atrial wall, ligating the vertical vein, and closing the atrial septal defect.

Postoperative pulmonary vein stenosis occurs in 5 to 10 percent of patients due to intimal hyperplasia and progressive fibromuscular proliferation at the anastomotic site, carrying high reoperation rates.

modules.name: Atrioventricular Septal Defects: Primum ASD, Cleft Mitral and Complete AV Canal Repair

topics.book: Sabiston Surgery 22e Ch 113 (Atrioventricular Septal Defect)

mustKnow.fact: Atrioventricular septal defects result from failure of fusion of the embryonic superior and inferior endocardial cushions, characterized by a common atrioventricular valve junction and an unwound, elongated left ventricular outflow tract.

Partial AV canal (primum ASD) consists of an ostium primum atrial septal defect, two separate atrioventricular valve orifices, and a characteristic cleft in the anterior mitral valve leaflet pointing toward the ventricular septum.

Complete atrioventricular canal defect features a confluent ostium primum ASD, an unrestrictive inlet VSD, and a single common atrioventricular valve orifice with five leaflets spanning both ventricles.

Complete AV canal defect is present in up to 40 percent of patients with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), who have an increased propensity for accelerated pulmonary vascular obstructive disease requiring repair by 3 to 6 months of age.

The Rastelli classification categorizes complete AV canal based on the morphology and chordal attachments of the common anterior bridging leaflet into Type A (tethered to crest of septum), Type B (tethered to RV), and Type C (free-floating).
